requirements.nl_text: Request Number - 328 | Request Title - Feature request: Sending dummy short messages | Request Description - TextSecure could mask meaningful communication between people by occasionally sending dummy random messages to random recipients at random times:  Recipients would be chosen randomly between contacts that knowingly use TextSecure, so it could be recognized as such after decryption and automatically discarded by recipient. "Randomness" should be tweaked to level-out the legitimate messages, spoiling the traffic analysis of traffic retention data, preventing to weigh connections in the deducted social network graph or guessing sleeping/activity patterns. People often have many unused messages in their monthly quota, so those could easily be used with no extra cost, or they value their privacy more than some money. Sender would need to enable this feature (opt-in) and define desired quantity (eg max 100 dummy messages per month, 2 dummy messages for every legitimate one, max 500 messages total counting legitimate and dummy ones...). The feature would need to be aware of roaming (disabled by default, optionally enable) and battery level (do not send if bellow eg. 30%). http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traffic_analysis#Countermeasures Possible extensions:  Recipients could be able to let their peers know, that they do not want to participate in this and do not want to receive messages for whatever reason (opt-out). Recipients could also be chosen randomly between other contacts (those not using TextSecure yet) to promote its use (default message) or a custom explanation by sender. Those messages would be in clear text. As this might be annoying it should be very limited (eg max 1 message to a single recipient per month, only during daytime...) to not be too intrusive spam. Dummy messages could contain other peer's phone numbers (random selection from those participating in dummy messaging, not just their contacts), never to be shown to user, just to send dummy messages to, to further mask the real social network. It would be tricky to opt-out later on once your number starts circulating, so opt-outs would need to be spread this way as well and by direct reply dummy message or by defining a TTL of each such number.

verdict.text:
## Summary
Opus/cot returned the right number of units for all 15 non-atomic requirements, but its slot behaviour is the reverse of the risk under test. It under-fills rather than fabricates: it marks the implied actor and modal verb as missing in most units, and it drops scope/condition placeholders entirely. The scorer then reads those dropped placeholders as "silently filled". Most of the headline Track 1 and Paska failures come from this convention mismatch, not from invented content.

## Missing-slot detection
Scope (42 gold-missing) and condition (14) are the only slots with support. Their apparent silent-fill rates are largely an artifact. The 802 examples read `<MISSING_ACTOR> <MISSING_MODAL_VERB> export …`, with no scope or condition text and no placeholder. The scorer counts that absence as "filled".

All 9 condition "fills" fall on 802#1–6, 222#1 and 226#1–2. The 25 scope "fills" cluster by whole requirement (802, 328, 222, 6424, 6390, 7567, 5904, 226). That clustering points to a per-requirement output-format choice, not per-unit fabrication. Real scope invention cannot be ruled out without reading the text, especially for 6424, where every slot was filled and similarity is low.

The one condition false positive (1692#2) is a genuine over-flag of a stated condition.

Actor, modalVerb and action have zero support, so their F1 of 0.0 means nothing. Their false positives are still informative. The model flagged the implied actor in 18 units and the implied modal in 30, where annotators wrote "the App must let the user". This over-flagging drives 34 of 42 incomplete verdicts against all-complete gold.

## Conversion quality
Similarity reaches about 79% of the human-human ceiling on seq_ratio and about 86% on cosine. Much of the gap is template text: humans emit `<MISSING_SCOPE>, <MISSING_CONDITION>, the App must…`, while the model emits actor/modal placeholders instead.

The genuine content outliers are 6390#1–2, 5904#1–2 and 6424#1–3, all below 0.46.

Paska mostly re-detects the model's own placeholders. Units the model judged complete pass at 75%; units it judged incomplete pass at 9%. "Not requirement", "Incomplete requirement" and "Incomplete system response" all follow from the missing actor/modal. The genuine Rimay defects are:
- condition placed after the system response (6424#1–2);
- passive voice (6390#1);
- condition without an actor (1692#1, 222#2–3).

## Units and atomicity
Count compliance is perfect at 15/15. Non-atomic detection is trivially 1.0, because the prompt states both atomicity and unit count, so it carries no signal here. The 2 reorderings appear to be 802 and 6424, judging by swapped segment ids. Alignment absorbed them, and neither affects the metrics.

## Anomalies
- None. The anomaly log does not detect omitted scope/condition placeholders, which is the dominant output pattern in this run.

## Next step
- Change the scorer to treat an absent scope/condition clause as "missing", or reject outputs lacking all five slot markers. Then rescore before comparing strategies.
- Align the prompt with the gold convention: always emit `<MISSING_SCOPE>`/`<MISSING_CONDITION>`, and fill an implied system actor and "must" rather than flagging them.
- Manually read 6424, 6390 and 5904 to separate real content divergence or invented scope from formatting noise.
